profiles.summary: The interpreter and the compiled code path of the Monad client call the same runtime functions for TSTORE, TLOAD, SLOAD, SSTORE, CALL and STATICCALL, so the PoolManager's transient accounting does not depend on which path runs. The deployed PoolManager returned the same amounts as reth for 600 simulated swaps once it had enough gas. The self-destruct result that the critic could not explain comes from how eth_call applies state overrides.

deltas.delta: The compiler emits a call to runtime::tload and runtime::tstore for the TLoad and TStore instructions (compiler/ir/x86.cpp lines 250 to 254, emitter.hpp lines 494 to 500). The interpreter calls the same two functions (instruction_table.hpp lines 1357 to 1389). Both read and write host transient storage under the address of the executing account, and tstore exits with an error under a static call (runtime/storage.hpp lines 38 to 62). The emitter uses the shared runtime functions for selfbalance, sload, sstore, mcopy, call and staticcall as well (emitter.hpp lines 470 to 573).
deltas.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/runtime/storage.hpp, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/compiler/ir/x86/emitter.hpp, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/compiler/ir/x86.cpp and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/interpreter/instruction_table.hpp

deltas.delta: Differential run on deployed bytecode. 600 calls to the deployed Quoter (quoteExactInputSingle and quoteExactOutputSingle, both directions, five sizes from 0.001 to 100,000 tokens) on 30 pools without hooks were executed by the Monad node at block 124,613,635. For each call the storage that the PoolManager read was taken from the Monad prestate tracer and placed, with the Monad PoolManager and Quoter code, at the same two addresses on an Ethereum node (reth v2.11.0) by state override. 556 calls gave the same first return word or the same revert data on both nodes (517 amounts, 495 of them distinct, and 39 reverts). The other 44 calls, in 15 pools, ran out of gas on Monad at 25 million gas while reth finished below 25 million. One of them was tried at 30 million gas, the cap of a Monad transaction, and failed there too. All 44 gave the reth result on Monad at 100 million gas. Each of them walks about 2,000 storage slots.

deltas.delta: SELFDESTRUCT with the contract itself as beneficiary removes the balance only when the account was created in the current transaction (State::selfdestruct_to_self_burns returns is_current_incarnation, state.cpp lines 448 to 480). eth_call applies state overrides with the same incarnation as the call itself and creates a missing override account in that step (monad_executor.cpp lines 163 to 175 and 258 to 261). An override contract therefore counts as created in the call, and its self-destruct burns the balance. This explains the balance of 0 that the cycle 3 probe saw on Monad. It is a property of the simulation path. The PoolManager bytecode has no SELFDESTRUCT.

findings.title: A two signature Safe can pause ten wrapped stock tokens or list the PoolManager as sanctioned, which would stop pools that hold 7.9 million dollars on Monad
findings.difference: On Monad the second largest asset class at the PoolManager is a set of wrapped stock tokens (wSPYx, wSPCXx, wTSLAx, wQQQx, wEWYx, wSMHx, wNVDAx, wSKHYx, wMUx, wANTx). The PoolManager holds between 89.4 and 99.8 percent of the supply of each. Every transfer of these tokens checks a pause flag and a sanctions list that the issuer controls. cbBTC on Monad adds freeze, pause and burn roles. The exposure comes from the tokens that make up the pooled value on this network. The Monad client plays no part in it.
findings.mechanism: 1. All pools of a currency share one balance at the PoolManager address, and take pays out with currency.transfer and reverts when the token call fails (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). 2. The wrapper's transfer hook requires that isPaused is false and that neither sender nor recipient is on the sanctions list of the underlying stock token (WrappedBackedTokenImplementation.sol lines 178 to 193). 3. setPause can be called by the pauser, a Safe with threshold 2 of 4. The sanctions list at 0x615dd3b9445a94334c1579f68115042d77cc7c44 has addToSanctionsList and is owned by a Safe with threshold 2 of 3, which also owns the wrappers and the proxy admin and can replace the wrapper code. 4. If the pauser pauses a wrapper, or the owner lists the PoolManager address, every take of that wrapper reverts, so no liquidity removal and no swap that pays out the wrapper can settle in any pool of that token. Transfers into the PoolManager revert as well, so settle cannot be funded. 5. isPaused is false for all ten wrappers and isSanctioned(PoolManager) is false today. 6. cbBTC (40.0 coins at the PoolManager, 43 percent of supply) has freeze(address), pause() and burn(address,uint256) behind FREEZER_ROLE, PAUSER_ROLE and BURNER_ROLE. A freeze of the PoolManager or a pause has the same effect, and a burn would leave pool accounting above the balance. 7. A live example of this class exists at small size. Curvance has paused the market manager 0xbc4cd7bbd8d38027a88838b88ba04561fa778c35, and a transfer of cWBTC or ceBTC from the PoolManager reverts today with MarketManager__Paused(). Five pools use each of the two tokens, and the PoolManager holds about 83 dollars of each. 8. No ordinary account can trigger any of these steps. A third party cannot move the PoolManager's wrapper shares, because redeem and withdraw spend an allowance of the owner (lines 265 to 273) and delegatedTransfer needs an ECDSA signature that recovers to the owner address (lines 112 to 131).
findings.impact: A pause or a sanctions entry freezes about 7.9 million dollars of wrapped stock tokens together with the other side of those pools while it lasts, for every liquidity provider in them. A freeze or pause of cbBTC does the same for about 2.5 million dollars of cbBTC. A burn of the PoolManager's cbBTC would leave the last providers unpaid. The Curvance pause already locks about 170 dollars.
findings.preconditions: Two signers of the pauser Safe or of the owner Safe act, or the holder of a cbBTC role acts. No action by an ordinary account leads there.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers should treat the issuer's pause and sanctions rights as a condition of these pools. The deployer can list these tokens in user documentation as issuer controlled. Core cannot route around a token that rejects transfers from the PoolManager.

findings.title: MegaETH blocks are not ordered by priority fee, so a queue of transactions that each fill the block budget for new state delays every later transaction by the length of the queue
findings.difference: MegaETH skips every candidate transaction of a block once the block has reached 1,000 new state entries, and its sequencer does not sort a block by priority fee. Ethereum has no per block cap on new state and orders by fee.
findings.mechanism: 1. BlockLimiter::pre_execution_check rejects every candidate once block_state_growth_used has reached the block limit of 1,000 (block/limit.rs lines 765 to 893), and the transaction that reaches the limit is itself included. Cycle 2 measured the cost of one such transaction at 22,559,525 gas, about 0.0000226 ETH at the base fee of 1,000,000 wei. 2. New in this cycle: in 232 of 300 sampled blocks a transaction with a lower priority fee sits ahead of one with a higher fee from another sender, so a user cannot move ahead of the filling transaction by paying more. 3. If the pool hands out pending transactions in arrival order and skipped ones keep their place, a sender who queues N filling transactions from several accounts closes N consecutive one second blocks, and a withdrawal that arrives later waits N blocks. The documentation allows 500 pending transactions per account and names no other rate limit. The sequencer's pool is not public, so this ordering is an inference from the block contents. 4. The delay is bounded by the queue that stood when the user's transaction arrived, and each second of delay costs the sender about 0.0000226 ETH. An hour costs about 0.08 ETH and a day about 1.95 ETH. 5. A liquidity removal or take through the PoolManager has no path around the limiter (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184, 291-297). 6. The L1 deposit route stays open. Deposits sit at index 1 in all 25 sampled deposit blocks, ahead of sequencer transactions, and the L1 portal sells at most 20,000,000 gas of deposits per L1 block, which pays for fewer than 900 new slots at about 22,500 gas each. The deposits of one L1 block can therefore not reach the limit of 1,000 before the last of them runs. 7. No use of this was found on chain: among 400,000 recent blocks the largest state growth of a traced heavy transaction is 27 entries.
findings.impact: No funds are lost. All users of the chain, including liquidity providers who want to withdraw, wait as long as the sender keeps a queue and pays for it. A user can leave through an L1 deposit, which costs L1 gas and lands within minutes.
findings.preconditions: The sender funds several accounts and pays about 0.0000226 ETH per second of delay. The sequencer keeps its present ordering and does not filter the sender.
findings.mitigations: Integrators who must exit under load can send the exit as an L1 deposit through the OptimismPortal. The operator can order or filter the pool so that transactions with large state growth do not come first in each block.

cleared.check: Transfer quotas, cooldowns and per block movement rules (lead L-259) for every token with a balance at the Monad PoolManager. Can a take of the whole balance that is paid back in the same unlock, repeated, leave the PoolManager unable to send (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-86)?
cleared.result: No token of size has such a rule. For 8,375 tokens the PoolManager address sent its whole balance to a second contract and received it back four times inside one call at block 124,612,088. 8,310 tokens completed all four rounds, and 8,017 of them also passed every other step with exact amounts, among them all 45 tokens with the largest pool reserves (USDC, syrupUSDC, GHO, mUSD, cbBTC, WBTC, AUSD, the wrapped stock tokens, WETH, apxUSD, WMON, USDT0, shMON). Of the 38 tokens that reject the first transfer, 36 are single pool creator tokens with their own gates (for example InvalidTransfer on BROKERSTR, OnlyController on a PKM token and the message Bot is not allowed on BATKNIGHT) and two are the paused Curvance tokens. Five tokens fail the return leg of the first round because they charge a fee or hold a few wei. For 22 single pool tokens the simulation ran out of gas, so they are untested. No token failed in a later round after passing the first, which is what a quota or cooldown would produce.

cleared.check: Wrapped stock tokens (lead L-259 names them): source of the wrapper for a limit on what one address may send or hold, and for a way in which another account can move or lock the PoolManager's shares.
cleared.result: The wrapper has no volume, count, cooldown or holding rule. _beforeTokenTransfer tests the pause flag and the sanctions list only (lines 178 to 193). redeem and withdraw by another account spend the owner's allowance, which the PoolManager never grants (lines 265 to 273). delegatedTransfer requires ECDSA recovery of the owner address (lines 112 to 131), and no signature recovers to a contract address. Conversion uses the multiplier of the underlying token and not the wrapper's holdings (lines 235 to 250), so a donation to the wrapper does not change what a share is worth. The four round test passed for all ten wrappers.

cleared.check: Curvance deposit tokens ask their market manager before each transfer. Can a third party put the PoolManager into a state in which that test fails for a while, for example by depositing for it (lead L-259)?
cleared.result: No. In a simulated call on cWMON (0x1e240e30e51491546dec3af16b0b4eac8dd110d4) a second account wrapped 1 MON and called deposit(assets, PoolManager) and mint(shares, PoolManager). Both succeeded and raised the PoolManager balance, and the PoolManager's transfers directly afterwards succeeded. depositAsCollateral, depositAsCollateralFor and repayFor with the PoolManager as account reverted for the third party. A zero amount transfer of these tokens reverts, which only affects a caller who asks for a zero take.

cleared.check: Balances that change without a transfer (lead L-172). Which pooled tokens move balanceOf(PoolManager) outside Transfer logs, and can an ordinary account raise such a balance between sync and settle and keep the credit (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364)?
cleared.result: Over one day 18 of 8,379 tokens did not reconcile and none of them is large. Aave deposit tokens (253.7 aMonUSDC and six below 3 units) and Neverland deposit tokens (24,696 nWMON, about 300 dollars, and smaller) grow with interest. The growth belongs to no pool and nobody can claim it, as recorded for other chains. The active case does not pay. On Aave the whole flash loan premium goes to the protocol, so the index does not move inside a transaction. On Neverland a share of each premium raises the index, and the PoolManager holds 0.044 percent of nWMON, so a caller who pays a premium of 0.5 percent on a loan would be credited at most 0.0002 percent of the loan. The four unwrapped stock tokens differ by 2 to 6 wei on balances of a few thousand wei. WMON differs because deposits emit no Transfer log.

cleared.check: Critic gap of cycle 2: does the compiled execution path of the Monad client treat TSTORE and TLOAD like the interpreter, so that the lock, the deltas and the synced reserves (src/libraries/Lock.sol:13-25, src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:21-39, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:17-36) behave the same whichever path runs the PoolManager?
cleared.result: Yes. Both paths call runtime::tstore and runtime::tload, which act on host transient storage under the address of the executing account, and tstore fails under a static call. The compiled path has no implementation of its own for these instructions or for SLOAD, SSTORE, CALL and STATICCALL.

cleared.check: Critic gap of cycle 3: the self-destruct probe left a balance of 0 on Monad for a contract that names itself as beneficiary. Is this a consensus rule that differs from Ethereum?
cleared.result: No. The client burns the balance only when the account was created in the current transaction, as EIP-6780 does. eth_call creates override accounts with the incarnation of the call, so the probe contract counted as created in the same transaction. A contract deployed in an earlier transaction keeps its balance.

cleared.check: A9 with measured numbers: can a swap that must cross a long run of initialized ticks fit under the 30 million gas cap of a Monad transaction?
cleared.result: A single transaction cannot walk a whole deep pool. 44 quotes that asked for more than 15 pools could supply needed more than 25 million and at most 100 million gas on Monad, each reading about 2,000 storage slots, while reth finished them below 25 million. The one case tried at the 30 million cap failed. A real swap stops at the caller's price limit (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344) and continues in the next transaction, and a liquidity removal touches two ticks. No withdrawal is blocked. This confirms the cycle 1 clearance with figures.

cleared.check: Lead L-171: are L1 deposits placed ahead of sequencer transactions, and can a deposit be skipped because the block's state growth counter has reached 1,000 while deposits remain?
cleared.result: Deposits come first. In 25 of 25 sampled deposit blocks the user deposit is at index 1, after the L1 attributes transaction and before every system and sequencer transaction, so the counter is near zero when deposits run. The OP Stack derivation rule places the user deposits of an L1 block in the first L2 block of its epoch. The L1 portal sells at most 20,000,000 gas of deposits per L1 block, and cycle 2 measured 20,333,678 gas for 900 new slots, so the deposits of one L1 block cannot create 1,000 entries. The limiter also applies its test before a transaction and admits the one that reaches the limit. A deposit can fail on its own transaction limits and is then included as failed with its mint kept.
cleared.source: https://megaeth.blockscout.com/api/v2/optimism/deposits, rpc https://mainnet.megaeth.com/rpc (eth_call with state overrides, eth_getLogs, eth_getBlockByNumber, eth_getBlockReceipts, eth_createAccessList, debug_traceTransaction) at blocks 32,206,276 to 32,609,052 on 2026-11-23, https://specs.optimism.io/protocol/derivation.html, rpc https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com resourceConfig() and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/megaeth-labs/mega-evm/main/crates/mega-evm/src/block/limit.rs lines 765 to 893

cleared.check: Lead L-251 and critic gap of cycle 3: does the KeylessDeploy sandbox start only at depth zero in the release that mainnet runs, and does any later specification or transaction type let it start next to other contract code of the same transaction (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364, 322-329)?
cleared.result: The depth test is present at tag v1.7.3, which the public stateless validator pins and uses to check every mainnet block. The file is byte identical to the main branch. The specification list ends at REX6 and the changelog of v1.7.3 records that REX7 was removed. The documented transaction types are legacy, EIP-2930, EIP-1559, EIP-7702 and deposit, each with one top-level call, and a delegated account whose code points at KeylessDeploy has a different target address, so the interceptor does not match it. The dependency line of the closed mega-reth binary was not read. That the validator agrees with the node on state roots is taken from the documentation and was not run here.

cleared.check: Lead L-213 for MegaETH: does the execution layer contain a rule that turns a user deposit into a failed deposit or leaves it out because of its sender or target, as the X Layer client does?
cleared.result: No such rule exists in mega-evm. The handler hook before_run treats only transactions sent from the system address specially and restricts them to the Oracle contract (evm/execution.rs lines 87 to 157, system/tx.rs line 25). The block executor passes deposits through the same limiter as other transactions and exempts them from the data availability tests (block/executor.rs lines 489 to 530, block/limit.rs lines 822 and 924). The files contain no list of blocked senders or targets. A deposit fails only on the per transaction resource limits that apply to every transaction. The payload builder of mega-reth is closed source and was not read.

leads.question: In which order does the MegaETH sequencer take pending transactions, and does a transaction that was skipped for a block level limit keep its place ahead of later arrivals? Ask the operator, or watch the mini-block stream while two accounts send marked transactions in a known order.
leads.why: Blocks are not sorted by priority fee. Under arrival order a queue of state filling transactions delays everyone by its length, which is what F-042 now assumes. Measuring it needs sent transactions, which this review does not do.

leads.question: Does the wrapped stock token implementation at 0x76c6851ea0b2741eedcbbed240715e8817e85583 compile from WrappedBackedTokenImplementation.sol of the Backed repository? Its 46 selectors match. The bytecode was not compared because no compiler is installed, and the contract is not verified on Sourcify.
leads.why: The clearance of quotas and third party moves for 7.9 million dollars of pooled tokens rests on that source.

Which of them hold PoolManager claims or can change fees or block removals for pools with pooled value?
leads.why: Hook risk is recorded in general as F-004. The hooks that carry most Monad pools were never read.

leadResults.answer: Monad part. No pooled token of size limits what one address may send or hold over a period. For all 8,375 tokens with a balance the PoolManager address sent its whole balance out and received it back four times in one simulated call. 8,310 complete all rounds, including the 45 tokens with the largest reserves, and 22 single pool tokens ran out of gas in simulation. The 38 tokens that reject a transfer do so on the first attempt because of creator gates or the Curvance pause, which is no quota. The wrapped stock tokens were read from source: the transfer hook tests pause and the sanctions list only. A third party deposit into a Curvance market for the PoolManager does not start a hold period for it. The network level part is covered by the cycle 1 clearance that the reserve balance rule skips accounts with contract code. MegaETH is not named in the lead. Its 67 tokens pass the same test, and its block budget for new state is F-042.

The order is not by priority fee. In 232 of 300 sampled blocks a transaction with a lower priority fee precedes one with a higher fee from another sender (525 of 3,316 neighbouring pairs). That fits arrival order per mini-block. Whether skipped transactions keep their place could not be established, because the sequencer's pool is closed source, the documentation is silent, and no block with a full state budget exists in 400,000 recent blocks to observe.

Deposits sit at index 1 in 25 of 25 sampled deposit blocks, ahead of system and sequencer transactions. One L1 block can carry at most 20,000,000 gas of deposits (resourceConfig on the L1 SystemConfig), which pays for fewer than 900 new slots, so deposits alone cannot bring the counter to 1,000, and the transaction that reaches the limit is itself admitted. The forced inclusion route of F-017 has no gap from this limit.

Enumerated from Initialize logs since deployment: 19,402 pools, 11,268 token currencies, 8,375 with a balance. New holdings of size are ten wrapped stock tokens worth 7.9 million dollars, 40 cbBTC, 337 bridged WETH and 1.7 WBTC. The wrapped stock tokens and cbBTC carry pause, sanctions, freeze and burn rights and are added to F-015. No second entry point to a pooled balance and no mirror of the native balance was found. Balances that change without transfers are Aave and Neverland deposit tokens with at most 24,696 nWMON (about 300 dollars) and unwrapped stock tokens at dust size.

Not observed and not excluded. Blocks are not ordered by fee, so under arrival order a queue of N filling transactions from several accounts would hold N blocks and delay later arrivals by N seconds at about 0.0000226 ETH per second. The only documented pool limit is 500 pending transactions per account. The delay is bounded by the queue length at arrival and does not reach L1 deposits, which are placed first. F-042 is updated with this bound and stays low.

No example in either direction. Headers of blocks 32,206,276 to 32,606,276 were read. 359 blocks exceed 20 million gas. The 30 transactions above 12 million gas in blocks of 20 to 80 million gas were traced, and the largest state growth is 27 entries. The heavy transactions are contract deployments. Blocks before 32,206,276 were not scanned.

MegaETH part. mega-evm has no rule that fails or drops a deposit because of its sender or target. before_run handles only transactions from the system address, and the block executor sends deposits through the general limiter with an exemption from the data availability tests. A deposit fails only on resource limits that apply to its own execution. The closed mega-reth payload builder was not read. The other chains of this lead belong to other units.

The public stateless validator pins mega-evm v1.7.3, and the depth test at system/intercept.rs line 301 is identical at that tag and on main. The specification list ends at REX6 and v1.7.3 removed the REX7 draft. The five documented transaction types each have one top-level call. No path was found that starts a sandbox beside other contract code of the same transaction. The dependency line of mega-reth v2.2.3 itself is not public and stays unconfirmed.
